analysis.alternative: The online deficit could arise from routing during the switch, from differences in learned memories, or from their interaction; the existing comparisons do not establish which.
analysis.expected_evidence: If the deficit follows the training history under both frozen routing modes, that supports a learned-memory contribution. If it follows routing mode on both memory sets, that supports an inference contribution. A crossed or inconsistent pattern suggests an interaction or insufficient evidence.
analysis.followup_test: In toolkit/tests/agent_generated.rs, train parallel and single-timescale controls on paired development streams, then at each switch clone each model into both routing modes, reset beliefs, freeze learning, and replay the same first 100 events. Compare paired accuracies across the resulting 2×2 training-history-by-routing conditions, alongside online switch accuracy and B retention; expose minimal access in toolkit/src/agent_candidate.rs if needed. No additional evaluator is required.
analysis.hypothesis: Parallel routing changes the memories learned during training, contributing to the online switch-to-B deficit even when its isolated frozen-routing effect is small.
analysis.limitations: The proposed follow-up has not been executed. Ten-seed development results are exploratory; training-history effects include all consequences of the routing intervention, and reset, frozen probes do not reproduce online adaptation. The evaluation failure does not establish a mechanism.
analysis.observation: Evaluation failed only reversed_asym switch to B: candidate accuracy was 0.591 versus mixture 0.6165, a 2.55-point deficit against the 2-point limit. In the development replay, frozen routing differences were at most 1 point across switch comparisons, while online parallel routing was 7.1 points worse than the single-timescale control on unequal-noise switch to B.

idea.approach: Implemented single-timescale context routing with reversible per-entry consolidation: surprising observations assigned to a memory gradually restore its plasticity. Added a fixed-consolidation control and a crossed training-history-by-routing follow-up. The required offline tests passed.
idea.falsification: Compare reversible and fixed consolidation on paired streams for retention and switch accuracy; no retention benefit or slower adaptation would weigh against the proposal. In the crossed follow-up, a deficit following training history rather than frozen routing would support a learned-memory contribution to the earlier parallel-filter deficit. Any required mean accuracy more than two percentage points below the mixture fails the campaign criterion.
idea.hypothesis: Releasing consolidation when assigned observations repeatedly contradict a memory may allow stale rules to adapt while preserving protection against interference. The earlier parallel-filter switch deficit is observed; routing, learned-memory changes, and their interaction remain competing explanations.
idea.limitations: Surprise can reflect noise or an incorrect context assignment, so releasing consolidation may damage useful memories. The mechanism test verifies changed consolidation on a simple sequence, not improved accuracy. The crossed follow-up uses frozen, reset inference and cannot reproduce online adaptation. No candidate development or evaluation score was measured.
idea.question: Can surprise-sensitive consolidation preserve earlier rules while improving adaptation relative to fixed consolidation and the mixture baseline?
